summary: 6rd gives IPv6 access across an IPv4 access network using 6-in-4 tunnels from customer equipment. This informational RFC proposes Gateway-initiated 6rd, where the tunnels start at an operator-owned gateway instead, so customer equipment needs no changes and no IPv4 address for it.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of every home building its own bridge to the new road, the town builds one big bridge, so homes do not have to do anything.

questions: how does gi 6rd differ from basic 6rd
why does gi 6rd not require ipv4 addresses for customer devices
how are ipv6 prefixes structured in gi 6rd
subtitle: Deploying IPv6 across IPv4 networks using an operator gateway instead of customer equipment.

tldr.problem: Basic 6rd requires each customer device to have a public IPv4 address and to set up tunnels for IPv6, which wastes scarce IPv4 addresses. Operators facing rapid growth need IPv6 but cannot assign public IPv4 to every device.
tldr.mechanism: Gateway-initiated 6rd moves tunnel setup from the customer site to an operator-owned gateway. The gateway tunnels all IPv6 traffic between the customer and the IPv6 network, while customer devices need only standard IPv6 configuration. No IPv4 address is needed on customer equipment.
tldr.outcome: GI 6rd became an alternative IPv6 transition technique that is easier to deploy than basic 6rd and consumes fewer IPv4 addresses, though the approach concentrates tunnel burden on operator gateways.

facts.label: IPv4 addresses needed per customer
facts.value: Zero (vs. one per device in basic 6rd)

today: RFC 6654 is Informational and describes an alternative IPv6 transition technique. GI 6rd is less widely deployed than basic 6rd, but represents an important design pattern for transition scenarios where IPv4 addresses are scarce and operators control the network edge.

sections.title: IPv6 Transition and the IPv4 Address Shortage
sections.content:
IPv6 offers abundant address space, but many networks still run IPv4 at their access edges. Standard 6rd (RFC 5969) tunnels IPv6 traffic across IPv4 networks using customer edge devices (6rd-CE) that set up 6-in-4 tunnels. Each customer device needs a public IPv4 address for the tunnel, which is problematic when IPv4 addresses are scarce.

This problem is especially acute for operators in high-growth regions adding subscribers rapidly. Assigning public IPv4 to each new device drains the remaining IPv4 pool, accelerating the exhaustion crisis. Operators need a way to offer IPv6 without assigning IPv4 to customer equipment.

Gateway-initiated 6rd (GI 6rd) solves this by moving the tunnel responsibility from customer devices to a single gateway owned by the operator.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of each car being assigned a bridge pass, one bridge operator has a pass and lets all cars use the bridge.

sections.title: How Gateway-Initiated 6rd Works
sections.content:
In GI 6rd, the operator deploys a dual-stack gateway at the edge of its access network (typically collocated with the broadband network gateway). This gateway communicates with customer devices over IPv6 and tunnels their IPv6 traffic to a border router over IPv4.

Customer devices are assigned IPv6 prefixes and operate using standard IPv6 configuration (stateless autoconfiguration or DHCPv6). They send IPv6 packets normally, and the gateway intercepts them. The gateway encapsulates the IPv6 packets in IPv4 and sends them through the operator's IPv4 network to a border router, which decapsulates and forwards them to the IPv6 Internet.

Return traffic follows the reverse path: the border router encapsulates IPv6 packets in IPv4 and sends them back to the gateway, which decapsulates and delivers them to the customer device.

Importantly, customer devices do not need IPv4 addresses, and they do not need to understand tunneling. They operate as if the gateway is an IPv6 router on their local network.
sections.plainLanguage: The gateway is like a postal worker who speaks both your local language and the international language. You mail letters in your language, the worker translates them, sends them across the border, where another worker translates them back.

sections.title: Structuring IPv6 Prefixes for GI 6rd
sections.content:
IPv6 prefixes delegated to customers are carefully structured to encode the gateway's IPv4 address. The prefix contains several parts: a common prefix (the same across all customers and gateways), a gateway identifier (the last bits of the gateway's IPv4 address), a customer site index (a unique identifier for that customer at this gateway), and the host portion.

For example, with a common prefix of 29 bits, a 12-bit gateway identifier, and a 15-bit customer site index, the resulting structure is a /56 delegated prefix. This encoding allows the border router to extract the gateway's IPv4 address from an incoming IPv6 destination address, determine where to tunnel the packet, and allows the gateway to identify which customer the packet belongs to after decapsulation.

This clever encoding scheme is the key to GI 6rd's efficiency. By embedding addressing information in the prefix structure, routers can forward packets without maintaining large lookup tables.
sections.plainLanguage: The address is like a mailbox number that contains clues about which town it is in and which street: the first digits tell you the town, the middle digits tell you the block, and the last digits tell you the specific house.

sections.title: Differences from Basic 6rd
sections.content:
GI 6rd simplifies the deployment compared to RFC 5969 (basic 6rd). Customer equipment does not need to run DHCP to discover tunnel parameters or configuration; it only needs standard IPv6 autoconfiguration. There is no 6rd DHCPv6 option to implement.

Because all customer devices at a gateway use a single tunnel, the border router handles far fewer tunnels than in basic 6rd, where each customer device would have its own tunnel. This reduces the operational burden on the border router.

The scope of Neighbor Unreachability Detection (a mechanism for detecting when a neighbor is no longer reachable) is also simpler: it applies only between the customer and the gateway, not across the tunneled connection, because the gateway is the only IPv6 neighbor from the customer's perspective.
sections.plainLanguage: Basic 6rd is like every car driving with its own bridge pass; GI 6rd is like one shuttle bus carrying all cars across the bridge.
